papers.title: Improving Group Fairness in Knowledge Distillation via Laplace Approximation of Early Exits
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains compact student models from larger teachers. Because students learn simpler surface-level features in early layers, errors grow for groups whose labels spuriously correlate with input attributes, degrading group fairness even when overall accuracy is comparable. Early-Exit Neural Networks (EENNs) enable predictions at multiple intermediate layers; confidence margins from early exits have been used to reweight cross-entropy and distillation losses per instance. This paper proposes using Laplace-approximation-based, well-calibrated uncertainty estimates (rather than margins) to reweight hard/ambiguous instances and improve group fairness. They benchmark a BERT-based model on MultiNLI.
papers.role: Ground truth on the d1 intersection: it directly pairs early-exit/depth-adaptive inference with group-fairness mitigation.
papers.whyLatest: Probably the single closest prior work to d1's exact question. Within ~1 year of the window (May 2025); a cornerstone for the intersection even though slightly before the strict 1-yr cutoff.
papers.novelty: Uses Bayesian (Laplace) calibrated uncertainty from intermediate exits as a reweighting signal for fairness, positioning calibration of the exit signal as a fairness lever rather than a margins heuristic.
papers.weakness: Small scale (BERT on one multi-label benchmark), evaluates group fairness only via reweighting-driven accuracy, and does not measure per-group exit-depth/accuracy-vs-depth distributions under a fixed threshold.
papers.oneLiner: Calibrated uncertainty extracted at early exits can be used to reweight training and improve group fairness in distillation.
papers.keyFinding: Laplace-based calibrated uncertainty at early exits more robustly identifies difficult/ambiguous instances than margin-based approaches, improving group fairness on MultiNLI.
papers.implication: Suggests the exit-confidence signal is a legitimate fairness lever, motivating d1/d2: if calibration at exits is already used to improve fairness, a shared threshold may not exit at equal true-error across groups.
papers.contributions: Proposes Laplace-approximation loss reweighting from early exits; benchmarks group-fairness impact vs. margin-based baselines; links EENN exits to fairness.
papers.methods: Early-Exit Neural Networks; Laplace approximation for calibrated uncertainty; per-instance reweighting of cross-entropy and distillation losses; BERT student/teacher on MultiNLI.
papers.experiments: BERT-based KD on MultiNLI; comparison of Laplace vs. confidence-margin reweighting for group fairness.
papers.results: Laplace-based reweighting improves group fairness relative to margin-based and baseline KD while keeping accuracy comparable.
papers.limitations: Single dataset/domain; no explicit per-group exit-depth or accuracy-vs-depth analysis; no fixed-shared-threshold fairness audit; NLU classification only, not generation.
papers.futureDirections: Measure per-group exit-depth distributions and accuracy-vs-depth curves under one shared threshold; extend to generative LLMs and demographic-annotated benchmarks.
papers.insights: The risk in d1's cheap test is real: the exit-confidence signal is already a fairness-relevant quantity, so a shared exit threshold plausibly creates a per-group gap.
papers.relevance: A-1 (core). Directly establishes early-exit + group fairness as connected, giving d1 a concrete anchor and confirming the mechanism (calibrated exit signal) that d2 formalizes.

papers.title: Beyond Greedy Exits: Improved Early Exit Decisions for Risk Control and Reliability
papers.abstract: Early-Exit Deep Neural Networks allow adaptive inference by predicting at intermediate layers, cutting cost and latency. Most strategies greedily exit when confidence exceeds a threshold fixed on a static validation set, which is problematic because the model can be overconfident in a wrong class and is not robust to distribution shift. The authors propose UAT, which adapts the exit threshold online with a Multi-Armed Bandit framework, using a reward function that assesses predictive certainty and its reliability to balance efficiency and quality while penalizing unnecessary late exits. They provide risk guarantees and validate on vision-language understanding, text generation, and classification, achieving 1.70-2.10x speedup with <2% accuracy drop.
papers.role: Mechanism / threshold-control: shows the exit threshold is already an adaptive, per-instance decision rather than a fixed shared rule.
papers.whyLatest: In-window (Sep 2025). Directly about how exit thresholds are chosen — the very object d1 asks whether it treats groups differently.
papers.novelty: Replaces static thresholds with an online, uncertainty-aware bandit that trades efficiency vs. reliability, and provides theoretical risk guarantees.
papers.weakness: Focuses on reliability/risk and efficiency, not demographic groups; no per-group fairness analysis; risk guarantees are marginal, not per-group (so a group-gap could persist by construction).
papers.oneLiner: A bandit-based adaptive exit threshold improves reliability and speedup but keeps risk marginal rather than group-wise.
papers.keyFinding: Adaptive, uncertainty-aware exit (UAT) yields 1.70-2.10x speedup with <2% drop and stronger risk control than static-threshold greedy exits.
papers.implication: Exit decision is a dynamic per-instance function; if the confidence signal is group-correlated, the adaptive threshold inherits that — an open door for d1/d2.
papers.contributions: UAT online adaptive-exit algorithm; reward function scoring certainty+reliability; risk guarantees; validation across VL/classification/generation.
papers.methods: Multi-Armed Bandit; online threshold adaptation; uncertainty-aware reward; conformity/risk analysis.
papers.experiments: Vision-language understanding, text generation, and classification tasks comparing UAT to static-threshold early exits.
papers.results: Consistent 1.70-2.10x speedups and <2% accuracy drop vs. full model; improved robustness under distribution shift.
papers.limitations: Marginal (not per-group) risk guarantees; no demographic grouping or exit-depth distribution analysis; cannot detect whether one group systematically exits later/errored.
papers.futureDirections: Add per-group risk control and audit of exit-depth distributions across demographic groups under the adaptive threshold.
papers.insights: Because the threshold is learned online from a confidence signal, d1 should ask whether that signal is group-calibrated — linking d1 to d2.
papers.relevance: B. Useful as the current best model of the exit decision; supplies the mechanism and baseline that d1 must extend with per-group auditing.

papers.title: The Diminishing Returns of Early-Exit Decoding in Modern LLMs
papers.abstract: In LLM inference, early-exit stops computation at an intermediate layer once the prediction is sufficiently confident, reducing latency and cost. But modern LLMs use improved pretraining recipes and architectures that reduce layer redundancy, potentially limiting early-exit opportunities. The authors re-evaluate layer-wise early-exit in modern LLMs, analyze how intermediate representations evolve during training, introduce a metric for intrinsic early-exit suitability, and propose a benchmark for exploring early-exit benefits on different models/workloads. They find a diminishing trend in early-exit effectiveness across newer generations; dense transformers generally offer more early-exit potential than Mixture-of-Experts and State Space Models; larger (>20B) and base pretrained models show higher early-exit potential.
papers.role: Applicability / method boundary: quantifies when depth-adaptive compute is even feasible in modern LLMs.
papers.whyLatest: In-window (Mar 2026). Grounds d1 by showing early-exit potential is model- and architecture-dependent, so any group bias will be model-specific.
papers.novelty: Introduces a quantitative intrinsic early-exit-suitability metric and a comparative benchmark; explains diminishing returns via layer-redundancy reduction.
papers.weakness: Efficiency/suitability only — no fairness dimension; no per-group exit-depth or accuracy-vs-depth curves; ignores demographic stratification.
papers.oneLiner: Modern LLMs show diminishing and architecture-dependent early-exit potential.
papers.keyFinding: Early-exit usefulness is shrinking in newer models and depends on architecture (dense > MoE/SSM), scale (>20B) and tuning (base > tuned).
papers.implication: Any d1 fairness result is conditional on the model's early-exit suitability; a fairness gap may be negligible simply because the model rarely exits early.
papers.contributions: Intrinsic early-exit suitability metric; benchmark across architectures/scales; analysis of intermediate representation evolution.
papers.methods: Layer-wise early-exit re-evaluation; suitability metric; benchmarks across dense/MoE/SSM and 1B-70B+ scales.
papers.experiments: Cross-model, cross-architecture early-exit potential study on workload benchmarks.
papers.results: Diminishing early-exit effectiveness in newer generations; dense > MoE/SSM; >20B and base models yield higher early-exit potential.
papers.limitations: No fairness or demographic dimension; not a per-group study; suitability metric is accuracy-driven, not equity-driven.
papers.futureDirections: Combine suitability with per-group accuracy-vs-depth curves to see whether diminishing early-exit potential also shrinks/drives fairness gaps.
papers.insights: The plan's d1 cheap test must first check whether the model is early-exit-capable at all; otherwise a null fairness result is uninformative.
papers.relevance: B. Sets the feasibility condition for d1 and warns that a small measured fairness effect may be an artifact of low early-exit potential.

papers.title: SimLens for Early Exit in Large Language Models: Eliciting Accurate Latent Predictions with One More Token
papers.abstract: Intermediate-layer predictions in LLMs are informative but hard to decode accurately, especially at early layers. Lens-style methods typically use a direct linear readout that drifts from the model's eventual prediction. SimLens is a training-free decoder for single-token decision tasks that keeps only the start token and a candidate answer token and runs one lightweight continuation through the upper layers, recovering far more accurate latent predictions than direct linear decoding. Linear SimLens approximates entropy-based confidence, and SimExit combines both into a hybrid early-exit mechanism. On ARC, BoolQ, and HeadQA with LLaMA-7B/Vicuna-7B, SimLens improves Iso-Compute accuracy in all six settings (+0.43 average); SimExit yields 1.15x speedup at best-accuracy and 1.40x with up to 1-point accuracy drop.
papers.role: Mechanism: how an accurate, entropy-based confidence signal for early exit is obtained (the signal d1/d2 depends on).
papers.whyLatest: Jul 2025 (just at window edge). Demonstrates the modern confidence/exit estimation machinery in LLMs.
papers.novelty: Training-free 'one more token' continuation decoder to recover accurate latent predictions; linear approximation of entropy for confidence; hybrid exit.
papers.weakness: Single-token decision tasks only; no demographic/group analysis; no per-group exit-depth audit; assumes a single shared Iso-Compute benchmark.
papers.oneLiner: A training-free decoder yields accurate intermediate-layer predictions and an entropy-based confidence signal for early exit.
papers.keyFinding: SimLens recovers accurate intermediate predictions and improves Iso-Compute accuracy; SimExit gives ~1.15-1.40x speedup at controlled accuracy.
papers.implication: The exit signal (entropy/confidence) is now well-defined and accurate enough for d1 to compute per-group accuracy-vs-depth curves on it.
papers.contributions: SimLens decoder; Linear SimLens entropy approximation; SimExit hybrid exit; Iso-Compute evaluation.
papers.methods: Training-free continuation decoding; entropy-based confidence; hybrid early-exit; Iso-Compute comparison.
papers.experiments: ARC, BoolQ, HeadQA with LLaMA-7B and Vicuna-7B.
papers.results: +0.43 average Iso-Compute accuracy gain; 1.15x speedup at best accuracy, 1.40x with 1 point drop.
papers.limitations: Single-token classification only; no groups; no fairness metrics; not demonstrated on generation or demographic datasets.
papers.futureDirections: Apply to demographic-annotated generation benchmarks and measure per-group exit-depth/accuracy-vs-depth under a shared threshold.
papers.insights: Provides the instrumental basis for d1's cheap test: an accurate confidence/entropy signal at intermediate layers is achievable, making per-group exit-depth measurement feasible.
papers.relevance: B. Methodological enabler for d1 (and d2) rather than a fairness result; good baseline for the accuracy-vs-depth measurement.

papers.title: HALF: Harm-Aware LLM Fairness Evaluation Aligned with Deployment
papers.abstract: LLMs are increasingly deployed in high-impact domains (clinical, legal, hiring, education), making pre-deployment fairness/bias evaluation critical. Existing evaluations are not grounded in real scenarios and ignore harm-severity differences (e.g., a biased surgical decision should not be weighted like a stylistic summarization bias). HALF (Harm-Aware LLM Fairness) assesses model bias in realistic applications and weighs outcomes by harm severity, organizing nine application domains into three tiers (Severe/Moderate/Mild) via a five-stage pipeline. Across eight LLMs, they find (1) LLMs are not consistently fair across domains, (2) model size/performance do not guarantee fairness, and (3) reasoning models do better in medical decision support but worse in education.
papers.role: Fairness measurement framing / benchmark: gives the deployment-aware per-domain fairness lens d1 needs.
papers.whyLatest: In-window (Oct 2025). Supplies the fairness-evaluation framing for d1's per-group quality question.
papers.novelty: Harm-severity-weighted, deployment-domain-aligned fairness evaluation with a three-tier harm taxonomy and staged pipeline.
papers.weakness: No adaptive-inference/depth dimension; not about exit-depth or per-group compute; harm weighting is opinion-derived and domain-level not group-level.
papers.oneLiner: A deployment-aligned, harm-weighted framework shows LLM fairness is uneven across domains and not guaranteed by scale.
papers.keyFinding: Fairness is domain-contingent and not guaranteed by model size/performance; reasoning models vary by domain (good in medical, worse in education).
papers.implication: For d1, per-group fairness of adaptive compute must be assessed within deployment context and by harm severity, not just aggregate metrics.
papers.contributions: HALF benchmark; three-tier harm taxonomy; five-stage pipeline; eight-model evaluation across nine domains.
papers.methods: Harm-severity tiering; domain-grounded bias evaluation; multi-model comparison.
papers.experiments: Eight LLMs across nine domains and three harm tiers.
papers.results: LLMs not consistently fair across domains; scale/performance don't ensure fairness; domain-dependent reasoning-model tradeoffs.
papers.limitations: No compute/adaptive-inference axis; per-domain harm weights rather than per-group; no exit-depth or per-group accuracy-vs-depth measurement.
papers.futureDirections: Fold adaptive-inference budget into harm-weighted evaluation; add per-group exit-depth and quality-gap metrics.
papers.insights: Reinforces d1's premise that a single aggregate fairness number hides subgroup/deployment gaps — the per-group gap the plan hypothesizes is plausible and under-measured.
papers.relevance: B. Supplies the deployment-aware fairness lens and benchmark scaffolding for d1 without addressing adaptive compute itself.

papers.title: Mixture-of-Recursions: Learning Dynamic Recursive Depths for Adaptive Token-Level Computation
papers.abstract: Scaling LLMs is expensive. Existing efficiency efforts target either parameter sharing or adaptive computation, but rarely both. Mixture-of-Recursions (MoR) combines both axes in a single Recursive Transformer: it reuses a shared stack of layers across recursion steps for parameter efficiency while lightweight routers adaptively assign different recursion depths to individual tokens (adaptive token-level thinking), focusing quadratic attention only among still-active tokens and caching only their KV pairs. A KV-sharing variant reuses KV pairs from the first recursion to cut memory. Across 135M-1.7B scales, MoR forms a new Pareto frontier, lowering validation perplexity and improving few-shot accuracy at equal training FLOPs while boosting throughput vs. vanilla/recursive baselines.
papers.role: Mechanism: dynamic token-level depth routing — the modern form of the adaptive-compute budget d1 asks about.
papers.whyLatest: Jul 2025 (window edge). Represents the current state of per-token adaptive depth allocation.
papers.novelty: Unifies parameter sharing and adaptive computation; learns per-token recursive depths with lightweight routers and selective KV caching.
papers.weakness: Purely efficiency/quality; no fairness dimension, no demographic analysis, no per-group allocation audit; routers trained on loss, not equity.
papers.oneLiner: Per-token depth routing boosts efficiency and quality but is trained without any group-fairness awareness.
papers.keyFinding: MoR sets a new Pareto frontier at 135M-1.7B scale: lower perplexity and better few-shot accuracy at equal FLOPs with higher throughput.
papers.implication: The mechanism that d1 must scrutinize — per-token/instance compute allocation — is now a trained router, so any group-correlation in that allocation is learned and thus auditable.
papers.contributions: MoR framework; per-token depth routers; selective KV caching; KV-sharing variant; Pareto analysis.
papers.methods: Recursive Transformer; token-level routing; selective KV caching; scaling study.
papers.experiments: 135M-1.7B models, perplexity and few-shot accuracy vs. vanilla and recursive baselines at matched FLOPs.
papers.results: New Pareto frontier; lower perplexity and higher few-shot accuracy at equal FLOPs with greater throughput.
papers.limitations: No fairness metrics or group analysis; token-level budgets not audited per demographic group; no generation-level demographic data.
papers.futureDirections: Audit learned per-token depth allocation across demographic groups; constrain routers to avoid group-correlated compute under-allocation.
papers.insights: Strengthens d1's motivation: adaptive compute is a learned per-instance allocation, so whether it under-serves groups is an empirical, testable question.
papers.relevance: C. Background mechanism; makes the adaptive-allocation object concrete but contains no fairness analysis.

papers.title: Token-Level Entropy Reveals Demographic Disparities in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: A name alone measurably reshapes a model's next-token distribution before any token is sampled. The authors measure full-vocabulary Shannon entropy of the next-token distribution across six open-weight model families on 5,760 sentence-completion prompts where race/gender are signaled only by a first name. Black-associated names co-occur with higher first-token entropy and more diverse continuations than White-associated names — directionally consistent in all six instruction-tuned models under shared raw-text input, all six base checkpoints, and (for output diversity) five of six models under native chat formatting — opposite to the homogeneity bias seen under explicit group labels. The gap persists under tokenization/frequency controls and on a frequency-matched subset; per-prompt effects are small (d=0.06-0.16) but uniformly signed (template-level paired d=0.66-1.08). Gender points the other way, additively with race. First-token entropy attenuates sharply under chat formatting, and explicit group-label probing is mostly null/reversed; a variance-matched comparison locates the output-diversity disparity in heterogeneity across name-conditioned continuations.
papers.role: Core evidence: the entropy/uncertainty signal that gates early exit is already group-differentiated.
papers.whyLatest: Foundation for d2 (Jan 2025). Establishes that the exit-driving signal (next-token entropy) varies by signaled demographic group.
papers.novelty: Shows a demographic disparity in the entropy of the token distribution itself, independent of explicit group labels, and shows probing methodology determines whether/which direction a disparity is detected.
papers.weakness: Sentence-completion entropy only; not tied to any early-exit/adaptive-compute policy; small per-prompt effects; no calibration/ECE analysis; chat-format dependence complicates generalization.
papers.oneLiner: LLM token-entropy is already differentiated by signaled race/gender, so a confidence-gated exit threshold may exit differently across groups.
papers.keyFinding: Black-associated names yield higher first-token entropy/diversity than White ones (uniformly signed across models), whereas explicit label probing is mostly null/reversed.
papers.implication: If entropy gates early exit (CALM/PABEE-style), a single shared threshold will not yield equal exit-depth or equal true-error across groups — the d2 hypothesis.
papers.contributions: Large-scale entropy-based disparity measurement; role of probing methodology; frequency- and tokenization-controlled analyses.
papers.methods: Full-vocabulary Shannon entropy; sentence-completion prompts differing only by first name; paired d-statistics; controls for tokenization/frequency.
papers.experiments: 6 model families × base + instruct checkpoints; 5,760 prompts; race/gender signaled by name; multiple formatting modes.
papers.results: Per-prompt d=0.06-0.16 but uniformly signed; template-level paired d=0.66-1.08; gender opposes race; gaps attenuate under chat formatting.
papers.limitations: No ECE/calibration or error-rate framing; no exit policy; generative diversity rather than accuracy; chat-format sensitivity limits robustness.
papers.futureDirections: Compute group-wise ECE/Brier of the exit-confidence signal and test whether per-group temperature scaling closes the gap while preserving overall calibration.
papers.insights: Directly supports the d2 cheap test: group-wise entropy/confidence is distinguishable, so group-conditional calibration is a plausible, measurable mitigation.
papers.relevance: A-1 (core, foundational). The empirical premise for d2 and the signal behind d1's exit decision.

papers.title: The Confidence Trap: Gender Bias and Predictive Certainty in LLMs
papers.abstract: As LLMs enter sensitive domains, how their confidence scores relate to fairness/bias matters. This study examines alignment between LLM-predicted confidence and human-annotated bias judgments, focusing on gender bias in gendered-pronoun-resolution contexts. It evaluates whether probability-confidence calibration metrics capture fairness-related disparities. Among six state-of-the-art models, Gemma-2 shows the worst calibration on the gender-bias benchmark. The main contribution is a fairness-aware evaluation of LLM confidence calibration plus a new calibration metric, Gender-ECE, designed to measure gender disparities in resolution tasks.
papers.role: Ground truth: a group-aware calibration metric (Gender-ECE) for the confidence signal, directly on-point for d2.
papers.whyLatest: In-window (Jan 2026). Introduces a group-conditional calibration metric exactly for d2's question.
papers.novelty: Introduces Gender-ECE, a group-specific expected-calibration-error metric, and evaluates confidence-vs-bias alignment across six models.
papers.weakness: Gendered-pronoun resolution only (binary gender, a narrow task); six models; no mitigation/intervention; not tied to an adaptive-exit confidence policy.
papers.oneLiner: A fairness-aware calibration metric (Gender-ECE) reveals that model confidence is group-miscalibrated on gender bias.
papers.keyFinding: Models differ sharply in gender calibration; Gemma-2 is worst; raw confidence calibration does not reflect gender fairness.
papers.implication: Shared confidence thresholds are group-miscalibrated on a protected dimension, amplifying the risk that adaptive-exit decisions discriminate.
papers.contributions: Gender-ECE metric; fairness-aware confidence calibration evaluation across six models.
papers.methods: Gendered pronoun resolution; probability-confidence calibration; gender-conditional ECE.
papers.experiments: Six state-of-the-art LLMs on a gender-bias benchmark with gendered pronoun resolution.
papers.results: Significant cross-model calibration differences; Gemma-2 worst; Gender-ECE captures disparities that aggregate ECE misses.
papers.limitations: Narrow task (pronoun resolution); binary gender; no per-group calibration intervention; not evaluated on generative open-ended output or adaptive-compute policies.
papers.futureDirections: Extend group-conditional ECE to generation and apply per-group temperature scaling/abstention to the exit confidence signal.
papers.insights: Provides the concrete group-calibration metric d2 needs and evidence that aggregate calibration can hide group miscalibration.
papers.relevance: A-1 (core). Supplies the measurement instrument and an empirical existence proof for group-wise confidence miscalibration.

papers.title: Hierarchical Group-Conditional Conformal Risk Control for Selective Prediction in Language Models
papers.abstract: LLMs serve heterogeneous populations structured by domain, topic difficulty, and linguistic style. Conformal risk control (CRC) gives rigorous marginal risk guarantees for selective prediction with abstention, but marginal guarantees do not imply per-group ones: a model can meet the population budget while systematically over-exposing subgroups to errors. Under mild shifts in group composition, standard CRC violates the budget in up to 47% of trials. HG-CRC (Hierarchical Group-Conditional CRC) is a post-hoc calibration framework enforcing simultaneous risk guarantees across all nodes of a user-defined group hierarchy, using a Bonferroni correction over nodes and a leaf-first policy that uses the most specific applicable threshold, backing off to coarser nodes when a finer one is uncertified or rejects the example. It needs only a held-out calibration set, no retraining. Evaluated on Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-3-4B over ARC Challenge and MMLU-Pro across eight configurations (IID, heterogeneity, mixture/domain/prompt/difficulty shift, label noise, quantization), HG-CRC reaches an empirical 0% violation rate and WGER=0 on ARC for high-accuracy models; results are benchmark-specific (MMLU-Pro models abstain entirely or retain WGER=0.014). Participation cost vs. global CRC is 22-37 points. Ablations show hierarchical depth clears the budget (removing difficulty level returns violations to ~11%); Bonferroni is needed for the guarantee though its empirical effect matters only with many nodes.
papers.role: Method / gold solution: post-hoc group-conditional calibration that enforces per-group risk on the abstention/exit decision.
papers.whyLatest: In-window (Jul 2026). The most direct existing answer to d2's group-conditional calibration question.
papers.novelty: Hierarchical group-conditional conformal risk control enforcing simultaneous per-group guarantees via Bonferroni + leaf-first threshold selection, post-hoc and calibration-only.
papers.weakness: Marginal-guarantee-forcing (not fairness-in-parity); high participation/coverage cost (22-37 points); still benchmark-specific; abstraction can trigger heavy abstention; not demographic-labeled fairness per se.
papers.oneLiner: Hierarchical group-conditional conformal risk control enforces per-group risk guarantees on selective prediction with abstention.
papers.keyFinding: HG-CRC reaches ~0% per-group violation (empirically) on ARC for well-calibrated models while standard CRC violates the budget in up to 47% of shifted trials.
papers.implication: Provides a concrete, testable mechanism for d2: group-conditional thresholding/calibration can flatten per-group error while preserving group safety.
papers.contributions: HG-CRC; hierarchical group hierarchy; Bonferroni-corrected node risk control; leaf-first threshold policy; calibration-only, no retraining.
papers.methods: Hierarchical group-conditional conformal risk; Bonferroni correction; leaf-first threshold policy; calibration set; WGER/risk metrics.
papers.experiments: Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Gemma-3-4B on ARC Challenge and MMLU-Pro across 8 configurations (IID, heterogeneity, mixture/domain/prompt/difficulty shift, label noise, quantization).
papers.results: 0% empirical violation & WGER=0 on ARC for high-accuracy models; benchmark-specific on MMLU-Pro; participation cost 22-37 points; removing hierarchy depth returns violations to ~11%.
papers.limitations: Risk-control (not parity/fairness) objective; coverage cost; benchmark/calibration-sensitivity; abstention-heavy on poorly calibrated models; not demographic-group fairness on generation.
papers.futureDirections: Reframe as group-wise calibration of the entropy gate; trade coverage vs. fairness; apply to demographic subgroups and generative exit policies.
papers.insights: Strongest evidence that group-conditional calibration of the confidence/abstention signal is achievable — the model d2 can adopt for the exit gate.
papers.relevance: A-1 (core/method). Provides the group-conditional calibration machinery d2 needs, and exposes its main cost (coverage).

papers.title: Fair and Calibrated Toxicity Detection with Robust Training and Abstention
papers.abstract: Fairness in toxicity classification spans three integrated axes: ranking, calibration, and abstention. Training-time interventions and post-hoc safety mechanisms cannot be evaluated independently because the former determines the latter's efficacy. The authors compare ERM, instance-level reweighting, and Group DRO across these axes, combined with temperature scaling, confidence-based abstention, and per-identity threshold optimization. Evaluation uses subgroup AUC, BPSN/BNSP AUC, error gaps, and per-subgroup ECE with bootstrap CIs (n=1000). Findings: (1) calibration disparity is a hidden fairness violation — ERM has near-perfect aggregate calibration (0.013) but is miscalibrated across all identity subgroups (+0.029 to +0.134); (2) training interventions reshape rather than eliminate disparity (reweighted ERM improves ranking but worsens the calibration-fairness gap by up to +0.232; Group DRO removes calibration disparity only by becoming uniformly miscalibrated, ECE 0.118); (3) post-hoc methods inherit training failure modes (temperature scaling fails because miscalibration is non-uniform; confidence abstention works under ERM but breaks under DRO where the risk-coverage curve rises with deferral); (4) abstention itself is unfair — confidence-based deferral helps background content far more than identity-mentioning content.
papers.role: Method + evidence: shows group-wise calibration disparity and that per-group abstention can itself be unfair — directly relevant to the exit/abstain gate.
papers.whyLatest: In-window (May 2026). Provides per-subgroup ECE and shows temperature scaling + abstention behave differently across groups.
papers.novelty: Jointly evaluates ranking, calibration, and abstention with per-subgroup ECE; shows training interventions reshape (not remove) calibration disparity and that abstention is itself group-unfair.
papers.weakness: Toxicity classification (not generation); per-identity rather than broad demographic groups; abstention is a yes/no safety decision, not a depth decision; small-scale.
papers.oneLiner: Calibration disparity is a hidden fairness violation, and confidence-based abstention can be unfair across groups.
papers.keyFinding: Aggregate calibration can look perfect (ECE 0.013) while all subgroups are miscalibrated; temperature scaling fails on non-uniform miscalibration; confidence abstention underperforms for identity-mentioning content.
papers.implication: For d2, both per-group calibration AND the abstention/exit decision itself can carry group bias — a shared exit threshold is doubly at risk.
papers.contributions: Multi-axis (ranking/calibration/abstention) fairness framework; per-subgroup ECE protocol; comparison of ERM/reweighting/Group DRO with post-hoc calibration.
papers.methods: ERM, instance reweighting, Group DRO; temperature scaling; confidence abstention; per-identity thresholds; subgroup ECE with bootstrap CIs.
papers.experiments: Toxicity classification with subgroup AUC, BPSN/BNSP AUC, error gaps, per-subgroup ECE (n=1000 bootstrap).
papers.results: ERM aggregate ECE 0.013 vs subgroup +0.029..+0.134; reweighting worsens calibration gap to +0.232; DRO removes disparity but ECE 0.118; abstention unfair (background>identity).
papers.limitations: Classification task; per-identity groups; abstention as binary safety decision; no generation or adaptive-depth; small datasets.
papers.futureDirections: Extend to demographic groups on generation; apply group-conditional calibration to a depth/exit gate; measure per-group coverage-exit curve.
papers.insights: Per-group calibration disparity + unfair abstention strongly motivate the plan's d2 hypothesis and give ready metric (per-subgroup ECE).
papers.relevance: A. Empirically demonstrates group-wise calibration disparity and the group-unfairness of abstention — core evidence for d2.

papers.title: Density Ridge Selective Prediction for LLM and VLM Hallucination Detection under Calibration Label Scarcity
papers.abstract: Hallucination detection is increasingly framed as selective prediction: an estimator scores confidence and abstains when low. Unsupervised sampling detectors (Semantic Entropy) avoid labels but plateau in quality, while supervised probes are strong in-distribution but degrade under calibration-label scarcity. The authors recover the response manifold as the density ridge of a kernel density estimate over a six-dimensional kinematic feature map of hidden-state generation trajectories, scoring a test generation by the negated Euclidean distance from its projected point to the nearest ridge vertex. Against Semantic Entropy, topological methods, and log-probability on six QA benchmarks (HaluEval-QA, TriviaQA, GSM8K, POPE, ScienceQA, A-OKVQA) with eight text/vision LLMs under a label-scarce protocol (n_cal=200, N=5 generations), the ridge score beats on AUROC by 5-20 points with tempered degradation under label scarcity.
papers.role: Calibration under scarcity: shows confidence/abstention quality degrades when calibration data is scarce — relevant to per-group calibration stability.
papers.whyLatest: In-window (Jun 2026). Provides a state-of-the-art selective-prediction/confidence estimator and a scarcity analysis that d2's per-group calibration must handle.
papers.novelty: Density-ridge geometric skeleton of the output distribution for confidence estimation; label-scarce selective prediction.
papers.weakness: No fairness/group dimension; hallucination-detection framing; no per-group calibration or demographic analysis; geometric estimator is domain-specific.
papers.oneLiner: A density-ridge confidence estimator is more accurate but still degrades under calibration-label scarcity.
papers.keyFinding: Density-ridge scoring beats Semantic Entropy/log-probability by 5-20 AUROC points and degrades more gracefully under label scarcity (n_cal=200).
papers.implication: Per-group calibration for small demographic groups will face label scarcity; this work shows which estimator degrades least and how much.
papers.contributions: Density-ridge confidence estimator; label-scarce selective-prediction protocol; comparison vs. entropy/topological/log-prob baselines.
papers.methods: KDE density ridge; 6D kinematic feature map of hidden-state trajectories; negated-distance scoring; selective prediction with abstention.
papers.experiments: Six QA benchmarks, eight text/VLM models, n_cal=200, N=5 generations.
papers.results: 5-20 point AUROC gain vs. baselines; tempered degradation under calibration-label scarcity.
papers.limitations: No group/fairness axis; hallucination detection only; small calibration budgets; no demographic stratification; not an early-exit/depth policy.
papers.futureDirections: Combine with group-conditional calibration to test whether minority-group confidence estimates are stable under scarcity.
papers.insights: Warns that d2's per-group calibration will be sample-starved for small groups; estimator choice and scarcity handling matter.
papers.relevance: B. Methodological complement for d2 (confidence estimation under scarce calibration data) but with no fairness dimension.

papers.title: Explaining How Quantization Disparately Skews a Model
papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is widely used for its high compression capacity, speed, and minimal accuracy impact. However, the authors observe that disparate impact is exacerbated by quantization, especially for minority groups. They explain that a chain of factors in forward and backward passes creates disparate impact across groups: changes in weights and activations from quantization cause cascaded network effects, lowering logit variance, increasing loss, and compromising group accuracies. They extend the study to the influence on group gradient norms and Hessian eigenvalues from an optimization perspective. To mitigate, they propose integrating mixed-precision quantization-aware training (QAT) with dataset sampling and weighted loss functions, enabling fairer deployment of quantized networks.
papers.role: Core mechanism: causal chain explaining WHY quantization redistributes error onto minority groups.
papers.whyLatest: In-window (Sep 2025). Gives the mechanistic explanation d3 needs for how compression redistributes error.
papers.novelty: Explains the disparate impact of quantization through a forward/backward causal chain (logit variance, loss, group accuracy, gradient norms, Hessian eigenvalues) and proposes a mixed-precision QAT + reweighting mitigation.
papers.weakness: Image/classification-oriented analysis; no open-ended generation or LLM benchmark; mechanism is optimization-theoretic, not evaluated on demographic LLM fairness datasets.
papers.oneLiner: Quantization cascades through the network to lower logit variance and worsen minority-group accuracy.
papers.keyFinding: Quantization-induced changes to weights/activations cascade to lower logit variance, higher loss, and compromised group accuracy, particularly for minority groups; mitigable via mixed-precision QAT + reweighting.
papers.implication: Provides the causal mechanism (logit-variance collapse) that d3 predicts also operates in depth-budgeted/early-exit inference.
papers.contributions: Causal explanation of quantization disparate impact; analysis of gradient norms/Hessian eigenvalues; mixed-precision QAT + sampling + weighted-loss mitigation.
papers.methods: PTQ analysis; forward/backward disparate-impact chain; gradient-norm and Hessian-eigenvalue optimization view; mixed-precision QAT with reweighting.
papers.experiments: Quantization disparate-impact study across groups; group accuracy, logit variance, loss, gradient norms, Hessian eigenvalues.
papers.results: Exacerbated disparate impact after quantization, especially minority groups; mitigation restores group accuracy with modest efficiency cost.
papers.limitations: Not an LLM generation/fairness benchmark; classification focus; mechanistic not end-to-end LLM social-bias evaluation.
papers.futureDirections: Test whether the same logit-variance/group-accuracy mechanism transfers to depth-budgeted (early-exit) inference.
papers.insights: Gives d3 a testable shared mechanism hypothesis — if quantization lowers logit variance and hurts minorities, early-exit (which also degrades shallow logits) might too.
papers.relevance: A-1 (core mechanism). The mechanistic backbone for d3; directly targestabishes the 'shared mechanism' hypothesis.

papers.title: Fair-GPTQ: Bias-Aware Quantization for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: The high memory demands of generative LLMs motivate quantization, which reduces memory by mapping weights to lower-precision integers. Recent empirical work shows quantization can increase the likelihood of biased outputs and degrade fairness benchmarks. This work links quantization and fairness by adding explicit group-fairness constraints to the quantization objective and introduces Fair-GPTQ, the first quantization method explicitly designed to reduce unfairness in LLMs. The added constraints guide the rounding operation toward less-biased text generation for protected groups, focusing on stereotype generation involving occupational bias and discriminatory language across gender, race, and religion. Fair-GPTQ has minimal accuracy impact (retains at least 90% of baseline accuracy on zero-shot benchmarks), reduces unfairness relative to a half-precision model, and preserves the memory/speed benefits of 4-bit quantization.
papers.role: Mitigation: a bias-aware compression method that reduces the fairness cost of quantization.
papers.whyLatest: In-window (Sep 2025). Provides the fairness-constrained compression method that d3's trade-off curve needs.
papers.novelty: First quantization method with explicit group-fairness constraints in the quantization objective (bias-aware rounding) for LLMs.
papers.weakness: Focuses on stereotype/occupational/discriminatory language (narrow bias types); no depth/early-exit dimension; accuracy-preservation floor of 90% is loose; limited model scale.
papers.oneLiner: Adding fairness constraints to the quantization objective reduces bias with minimal accuracy loss.
papers.keyFinding: Fair-GPTQ reduces unfairness vs. a half-precision model while retaining >=90% zero-shot accuracy and 4-bit memory/speed benefits.
papers.implication: Shows compression-induced unfairness is controllable at the objective level — a template for fairness-aware depth budgets in d3.
papers.contributions: Fair-GPTQ; group-fairness constraints in the quantization (rounding) objective; minimal-accuracy-cost bias reduction.
papers.methods: Group-fairness-constrained quantization; bias-aware rounding; zero-shot accuracy evaluation; fairness benchmarks for stereotypes/occupation/discrimination.
papers.experiments: LLM quantization with fairness constraints on stereotype/occupation/discrimination datasets vs. standard quantization and half-precision.
papers.results: Reduced unfairness relative to half-precision; >=90% baseline zero-shot accuracy; 4-bit memory/speed retained.
papers.limitations: Bias types limited to stereotype/occupational/discriminatory text; no depth-adaptive or early-exit comparison; no per-group accuracy-vs-depth measurement.
papers.futureDirections: Adapt the fairness-constrained objective to depth-budgeting (exit thresholds) and evaluate on per-group accuracy-vs-compression Pareto curves.
papers.insights: Demonstrates the fairness/efficiency trade-off is tractable via objective constraints — the template d3 wants for depth-budgeted inference.
papers.relevance: A-1 (core). Concrete compression-side fairness mitigation that d3 should port to the depth/exit budget.

papers.title: How Quantization Shapes Bias in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: This work comprehensively evaluates how quantization affects model bias, with attention to individual demographic subgroups. Focusing on weight and activation quantization strategies, it examines effects across a broad range of bias types — stereotypes, fairness, toxicity, sentiment — using both probability- and generated-text-based metrics across 13 benchmarks and models differing in architecture family and reasoning ability. Findings: quantization has a nuanced impact on bias — it can reduce toxicity and does not significantly affect sentiment, but tends to slightly increase stereotypes and unfairness in generative tasks, especially under aggressive compression. Trends are generally consistent across demographic categories/subgroups and model types, though magnitude depends on the specific setting.
papers.role: Evidence/measurement: large-scale benchmark establishing the direction and magnitude of compression-induced bias across subgroups.
papers.whyLatest: In-window (Aug 2025). Broad, benchmark-rich quantification of compression's effect on subgroup bias.
papers.novelty: Broadest quantitative sweep of quantization→bias across 13 benchmarks, multiple bias types, and per-subgroup breakdown, using both probability- and generated-text metrics.
papers.weakness: Reports average trends but notes magnitude varies by setting; does not isolate a mechanism; no early-exit/depth dimension; descriptive rather than causal.
papers.oneLiner: Quantization slightly increases stereotype/unfairness in generation while reducing toxicity, to varying degree by subgroup and setting.
papers.keyFinding: Aggressive quantization tends to increase stereotypes and unfairness in generative tasks, with subgroup- and model-dependent magnitudes; toxicity can decline.
papers.implication: Establishes that compression redistributes bias onto (generative) fairness dimensions, and that per-subgroup effects are real and heterogeneous.
papers.contributions: 13-benchmark, per-subgroup quantization→bias evaluation; probability- and text-based metrics; multiple architecture/reasoning settings.
papers.methods: Weight/activation quantization; stereotype/fairness/toxicity/sentiment metrics; per-demographic-subgroup breakdown.
papers.experiments: 13 benchmarks across quantization schemes and multiple models/demographic subgroups.
papers.results: Toxicity down, sentiment unaffected, stereotypes/unfairness slightly up under aggressive compression; trends consistent across subgroups but magnitude varies.
papers.limitations: Descriptive/aggregate; per-subgroup magnitudes vary by setting; no mechanistic isolation; no depth-budget/early-exit comparison.
papers.futureDirections: Link the per-subgroup magnitude variation to a mechanism (e.g., logit-variance collapse) and test transfer to depth-budgeted compute.
papers.insights: Supports d3's premise that compression rearranges subgroup error with misleadingly neutral aggregates — the measurement baseline d3's Pareto curve needs.
papers.relevance: A. Broad empirical grounding for compression-induced subgroup bias; complements the mechanistic papers.

papers.title: Uncertainty Drives Social Bias Changes in Quantized Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Post-training quantization cuts cost but fundamentally alters social biases in ways aggregate metrics miss. The authors present the first large-scale study of 50 quantized models on PostTrainingBiasBench, a unified benchmark of 13 closed- and open-ended bias datasets. They identify 'quantization-induced masked bias flipping', where up to 21% of responses flip between biased and unbiased states after quantization despite no change in aggregate bias scores. Flips are strongly driven by model uncertainty: high-uncertainty responses are 3-11x more likely to change than confident ones. Quantization strength amplifies this — 4-bit models show 4-6x more behavioral change than 8-bit. Critically, changes create asymmetric impacts across demographic groups, where bias can worsen by up to 18.6% for some groups while improving by 14.1% for others, yielding misleadingly neutral aggregate outcomes. Larger models show no consistent robustness advantage, and group-specific shifts vary unpredictably across model families.
papers.role: Mechanism + evidence: connects model uncertainty (the exit signal) to compression-induced, group-asymmetric bias change.
papers.whyLatest: In-window (Feb 2026). Most direct evidence that uncertainty drives group-asymmetric bias redististribution under compression — the d3/d2 bridge.
papers.novelty: Defines 'quantization-induced masked bias flipping'; ties it to model uncertainty; shows group-asymmetric (18.6% worse / 14.1% better) shifts that net to neutral in aggregate.
papers.weakness: Quantization-specific (not pruning/early-exit); uncertainty link is correlational; group-specific shifts vary unpredictably across models, limiting portability of conclusions.
papers.oneLiner: Quantization flips biases unpredictably and asymmetrically across groups, driven by uncertainty, even when aggregate bias is unchanged.
papers.keyFinding: Up to 21% of responses flip bias state with no aggregate change; uncertainty makes flips 3-11x more likely; asymmetric group impacts (+18.6% worse / -14.1% better) cancel in aggregate.
papers.implication: The uncertainty/confidence signal is the driver of compression-induced, group-asymmetric error — directly bridging d3 to d2 and to d1's entropy-gated exit.
papers.contributions: PostTrainingBiasBench (13 datasets); 50-model study; masked-bias-flipping phenomenon linked to uncertainty; group-asymmetry analysis.
papers.methods: Large-scale quantization study; response-level flipping detection; uncertainty-stratified analysis; per-group bias deltas.
papers.experiments: 50 quantized models across 13 closed/open-ended bias datasets; 4-bit vs 8-bit; per-group and per-family analysis.
papers.results: 21% flip rate despite flat aggregate; 3-11x flip likelihood for high-uncertainty; 4-6x more change at 4-bit; group asymmetry +18.6%/-14.1%; no large-model robustness advantage.
papers.limitations: Quantization only; uncertainty link correlational; group shifts unpredictable across families; no depth/early-exit or pruning comparison.
papers.futureDirections: Test whether the same uncertainty-driven, group-asymmetric redistribution appears under depth-budgeted (early-exit) compute and pruning.
papers.insights: Strongest bridge in the entire set: it says the confidence/uncertainty signal that gates exit is the same signal that drives group-asymmetric error under compression — the shared mechanism d3 posits.
papers.relevance: A-1 (core, bridging). Jointly supports d3 (compression redistributes to groups) and d2 (uncertainty drives it), implying depth-budgeted inference will also redistribute via uncertainty.

papers.title: The Impact of Inference Acceleration on Bias of LLMs
papers.abstract: LLMs are large and costly/slow to run, so a body of work proposes inference-efficiency strategies — quantization, pruning, and caching — that cut cost/latency by several factors while retaining much of benchmark accuracy. This work explores another performance dimension: demographic bias in model generations due to inference-acceleration optimizations. Using a wide range of metrics, they probe bias from many angles. Analysis before/after acceleration shows significant change in bias. Worryingly, these bias effects are complex and unpredictable: a given acceleration-strategy × bias-type combination may show little change in one model but a large effect in another. The results highlight a need for case-by-case evaluation of model bias after acceleration changes.
papers.role: Evidence: adaptive/accelerated inference (quantization, pruning, caching) changes demographic bias in model generations unpredictably.
papers.whyLatest: Foundation for d3 (Oct 2024). Across ~18 months but is a cornerstone of the compression→bias literature the plan builds on.
papers.novelty: Systematically evaluates how inference-acceleration strategies (not just accuracy) alter demographic bias, and shows the effects are strategy/model-specific and unpredictable.
papers.weakness: Older (outside strict window); observable-level and unpredictable; no mechanistic explanation; no per-group exit-depth or depth-budget analysis; acceleration strategies treated at a high level.
papers.oneLiner: Inference acceleration changes LLM bias in complex, model- and strategy-specific ways.
papers.keyFinding: Acceleration optimizations cause significant, unpredictable changes in demographic bias; effects vary by strategy-model-bias-type combination.
papers.implication: Adopting acceleration (including adaptive-depth) without per-group re-audit risks silent bias shifts — the practical motivation for d3 and d1.
papers.contributions: First systematic demographic-bias audit of inference-acceleration strategies; bias-metric suite; case-by-case evaluation recommendation.
papers.methods: Apply quantization/pruning/caching acceleration; measure demographic bias across multiple metrics; pre/post comparisons.
papers.experiments: Bias probe across several models, acceleration strategies, and bias metrics.
papers.results: Significant, unpredictable bias changes; small in some combinations, large in others, depending on strategy and model.
papers.limitations: No mechanism; no per-group exit-depth; acceleration measured broadly; not generative-fairness-specific; dated.
papers.futureDirections: Separate shared-mechanism from strategy-specific effects; add depth-budget/early-exit comparisons and per-group error Pareto curves.
papers.insights: Foundational for d3's thesis that efficiency gains carry hidden, group-dependent fairness costs that need dedicated evaluation.
papers.relevance: A-1 (foundational, slightly older). The anchor reference for d3's 'compression/efficiency redistributes bias' framing.
